extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates or beginning graduate students in algebraic topology and algebraic geometry (readers of Evan Chen's Napkin notes)
extracted.subtask_description: Expository textbook material defining and relating cohomology operations (cup product, cross product, cohomology rings, Künneth formula) and basic algebraic geometry notions (affine varieties, ideals, radicals, Nullstellensatz, Zariski topology, primes/maximals, motivation for schemes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative cup product
rubrics_metrics.description: For A ⊆ X, there is a relative cup product H^k(X,A;R) × H^ℓ(X,A;R) → H^{k+ℓ}(X,A;R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If either cochain vanishes on chains in A then so does their cup product; this lets one define relative cohomology pseudo-rings and reduced cohomology. (Context: §76.5)

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative cohomology pseudo-ring and reduced cohomology
rubrics_metrics.description: Define H•(X,A;R) = ⨁_{k≥0} H^k(X,A;R) and reduced cohomology ēH•(X;R) = ⨁_{k≥0} ēH^k(X;R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are anticommutative pseudo-rings; often ēH^0(X;R)=0 so there may be no multiplicative identity. Functoriality holds for these constructions. (§76.5)

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohomology (pseudo-)rings are functorial
rubrics_metrics.description: Fix a commutative ring R. The constructions H•(−;R) and H•(−,−;R) define functors H•(−;R): hTop^op → GradedRings and H•(−,−;R): hPairTop^op → GradedPseudoRings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This records that cohomology rings/pseudo-rings are natural with respect to maps of spaces and pairs. (Theorem 76.5.1)

rubrics_metrics.name: Product pseudo-ring of graded pseudo-rings
rubrics_metrics.description: Given graded pseudo-rings R and S, the product pseudo-ring R × S has underlying graded abelian group ⨁_{d≥0} (R_d ⊕ S_d), multiplication coming from R and S, and declare r·s = 0 for r∈R, s∈S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the graded analogue of the product ring; if R and S are graded rings with units, then R×S is a graded ring. (Definition 76.6.1 and Exercise 76.6.2)

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohomology pseudo-rings of wedge sums
rubrics_metrics.description: For spaces X,Y and ring R, ēH•(X ∨ Y; R) ≅ ēH•(X;R) × ēH•(Y;R) as graded pseudo-rings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The isomorphism is induced by embedding X and Y into the wedge and restricting cochains; it respects cup product. (Theorem 76.6.3)

rubrics_metrics.name: Isomorphism via restriction of cochains for wedge sums
rubrics_metrics.description: Given f ∈ C•(X∨Y;R), interpreting f as a cochain on X (via embedding) and similarly on Y yields the map ēH•(X∨Y;R) → ēH•(X;R) × ēH•(Y;R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explicit description lets you track generators and compute values (example: a cocycle on X∨Y may assign the sum of values from X and Y to the whole space).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cup product to distinguish spaces with same cohomology groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when H^n groups match for two spaces, their cohomology rings (cup products) can differ; e.g., H•(CP^2;Z) has α·α = α^2 ≠ 0, while in ēH•(S^2∨S^4;Z) the square of the degree-2 generator is 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequently CP^2 and S^2∨S^4 are not homotopy equivalent despite matching groups. Examples and exercises illustrate this distinction. (Example 76.6.4 and following)

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross product motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Intuition: if X has an m-dimensional hole and Y an n-dimensional hole, then X×Y has an (m+n)-dimensional hole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This motivates defining a cross product which pairs classes in H_m(X) and H_n(Y) to give a class in H_{m+n}(X×Y). (§76.7.i)

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross product on singular homology
rubrics_metrics.description: Define on simplices: for an m-simplex f:Δ^m→X and n-simplex g:Δ^n→Y, produce an (m+n)-chain f×g ∈ C_{m+n}(X×Y) by subdividing Δ^m × Δ^n into simplices; extend bilinearly to Cm×Cn → C_{m+n}(X×Y) and pass to homology to get H_m × H_n → H_{m+n}(X×Y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subdivision is combinatorially large in general; reference to Hatcher for formal construction. (§76.7.ii)

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross product is not a Z-module homomorphism (tensor fix)
rubrics_metrics.description: The naive × : C_m(X) × C_n(Y) → C_{m+n}(X×Y) is bilinear but not Z-linear when viewed as a map from the direct product; e.g., ×(2·(a,b)) ≠ 2×(a,b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fix by passing to the tensor product: define × : C_m(X) ⊗_Z C_n(Y) → C_{m+n}(X×Y), so ×(a⊗b)=a×b; similarly get × : H_m ⊗ H_n → H_{m+n}. This yields well-behaved module maps and injectivity statements under hypotheses. (Example 76.7.3 and Theorem 76.7.4)

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross product on cellular homology
rubrics_metrics.description: For CW complexes X and Y, give X×Y a CW structure whose cells are products of cells, and define × on cellular chain bases: e_m × e'_n = e_m × e'_n considered as a cell in X×Y, inducing × : H_m(X) ⊗ H_n(Y) → H_{m+n}(X×Y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This cellular definition is cleaner than the singular-simplice subdivision and agrees with it on homology. (§76.7.iv and Example 76.7.5)

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross product on cellular cohomology
rubrics_metrics.description: Given cellular cochains f ∈ Hom(Cells_m(X),R), g ∈ Hom(Cells_n(Y),R), define (f×g)(e_m × e_n) = f(e_m)·g(e_n) and set (f×g) to 0 on cells not decomposable as products; induces × : H^m(X;R) ⊗_R H^n(Y;R) → H^{m+n}(X×Y;R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mirrors the cellular homology product and avoids heavy subdivision. (§76.7.v)

rubrics_metrics.name: Wedge (cup/wedge) product via diagonal and cross product
rubrics_metrics.description: For vector space X and α ∈ (∧^m V(X))^∨, β ∈ (∧^n V(X))^∨, define α∧β = Δ^*(α×β) where Δ:X→X×X is the diagonal and Δ^* denotes pullback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently: evaluate α∧β on an (m+n)-wedge by pushing it to X×X and applying α×β. This connects the cross product and the wedge (cup) product in cohomology. (Definition 76.7.7 and §76.7.vi)

rubrics_metrics.name: Piecing cohomology groups into an algebra homomorphism
rubrics_metrics.description: Desire to extend the degreewise map × : H^m(X;R) ⊗ H^n(Y;R) → H^{m+n}(X×Y;R) to an R-algebra homomorphism × : H•(X;R) ⊗_R H•(Y;R) → H•(X×Y;R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires defining the tensor product of graded rings; multiplication must respect graded degrees. (§76.7.vii)

rubrics_metrics.name: Tensor product of graded rings
rubrics_metrics.description: For graded rings A and B (also R-modules), define (A⊗_R B)_d = ⨁_{k=0}^d A_k ⊗_R B_{d-k} with multiplication (a1⊗b1)(a2⊗b2) = (a1a2) ⊗ (b1b2) and unit 1_A ⊗ 1_B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the graded tensor product used when forming H•(X)⊗H•(Y). (Definition 76.8.1)

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross product via projections and cup product (cohomology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given projections π_X, π_Y from X×Y, define the cross product H•(X;R) ⊗_R H•(Y;R) → H•(X×Y;R) on cocycles by ϕ×ψ = π_X^*(ϕ) ⌣ π_Y^*(ψ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition coincides with the cellular definition; it yields a graded ring homomorphism. (Definition 76.8.2 and Remark 76.8.3)

rubrics_metrics.name: Künneth formula (special case / cohomology ring isomorphism)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X and Y are CW complexes and each H^k(Y;R) is a finitely generated free R-module, then the cross product gives an isomorphism of anticommutative rings H•(X;R) ⊗_R H•(Y;R) → H•(X×Y;R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under this hypothesis there is a one-to-one correspondence between pairs of generators (holes) in X and Y and generators in X×Y, compatible with cup product. (Theorem 76.8.4)

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of an affine variety V(S)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a set S of polynomials S ⊆ C[x1,...,xn], define V(S) as the set of points in A^n vanishing on all polynomials of S; such a set is an affine variety. (Definition 77.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: lines V(Ax+By+C), parabola V(y−x^2), hyperbola V(xy−1), axes V(xy), points V(x−x0,y−y0), whole space V(0), empty set V(1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming affine varieties via ideals (use ideals not generators)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given polynomials f1,...,fm, shorthand V(f1,...,fm) means V( (f1,...,fm) ), i.e., consider the ideal I they generate and take V(I).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because C[x1,...,xn] is Noetherian (Hilbert basis theorem), every ideal is finitely generated; using ideals gives more canonical naming than arbitrary generating sets. (§77.2, Abuse of Notation 77.2.4)

rubrics_metrics.name: Radical of an ideal and radical ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: For ring R and ideal I⊆R define √I = { r∈R | r^m ∈ I for some m≥1 }. An ideal I is radical if I = √I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties: √I is always radical; prime ideals are radical; for I⊆C[x1,...,xn], V(I) = V(√I). Number-theoretic analogy: √(12) = (6) in Z. (Definition 77.3.1 and Proposition 77.3.3)

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert's Nullstellensatz (varieties ↔ radical ideals)
rubrics_metrics.description: For affine variety V = V(I) in C[x1,...,xn], the set of polynomials vanishing on V is √I. Equivalently, V(I)=V(J) iff √I = √J; radical ideals in C[x1,...,xn] correspond exactly to affine varieties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This relies on C being algebraically closed. Weak Nullstellensatz (later) gives maximal ideals correspond to points. (Theorem 77.3.4)

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersections and finite unions of affine varieties
rubrics_metrics.description: Intersection of (even infinitely many) affine varieties is an affine variety; finite union of affine varieties is an affine variety. Formulas: V(∪_α I_α) = V(∩_α I_α) and ⋃_{k=1}^n V(I_k) = V(∩_{k=1}^n I_k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also V(−) is inclusion-reversing: I⊆J implies V(I) ⊇ V(J). Note: sum of ideals need not be radical. (Theorem 77.4.2, Remark 77.4.3, Proposition 77.4.4)

rubrics_metrics.name: Irreducible variety and prime ideals equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: A variety V is irreducible if it cannot be written as union of two proper subvarieties. For a radical ideal I with V=V(I) nonempty, I is prime iff V is irreducible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use set-theoretic arguments: if fg ∈ I then V ⊆ V(f)∪V(g) and irreducibility forces one factor to vanish on V. (Definition 77.5.1 and Theorem 77.5.5)

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximal ideals correspond to points (Weak Nullstellensatz)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every maximal ideal of C[x1,...,xn] is of the form (x1−a1,...,xn−an), so maximal ideals correspond to single points in C^n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This uses algebraically closed field property; e.g., (x^2+1) is maximal in R[x] but does not correspond to a real point. (Theorem 77.7.1)

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation for schemes: non-radical ideals capture multiplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Varieties (sets of points) cannot detect multiplicity; non-radical ideals encode multiplicity information. Example: (y−x^2) ∩ (y) at tangent intersection yields ideal (x^2,y) and quotient C[x,y]/(x^2,y) ≅ C[ε]/(ε^2), a 'double point'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To encode multiplicities one needs the finer notion of schemes (ringed spaces), not just varieties. (§77.8)

rubrics_metrics.name: Zariski topology on A^n
rubrics_metrics.description: Closed sets in the Zariski topology are sets of the form V(I) for ideals I⊆C[x1,...,xn]; open sets are their complements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In A^1 closed sets are finite sets of points (and ∅ and whole space); in A^2 closed sets include curves and points, so typical open sets are complements of finite unions of curves/points. This topology is very non-Hausdorff but natural for algebraic geometry. (Definition 78.2.1, Examples 78.2.2 and 78.2.3)
